issues.description: Omission of key demographic covariates: The cross-lagged panel model appears to only include SDO, RWA, and environmentalism, without adjusting for key demographic covariates such as gender, age, or socioeconomic status. Given that the literature establishes significant demographic differences in both ideological orientations (e.g., the "conservative male effect" cited in the manuscript) and environmental attitudes, failing to control for these variables leaves the model vulnerable to spurious associations. The authors should incorporate relevant demographic covariates into their path analysis to ensure the robustness of the cross-lagged effects.

issues.description: Unjustified causal claims: The authors use cross-lagged panel analysis on observational survey data to infer a "causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism." While cross-lagged models can establish temporal precedence, they cannot definitively prove causality due to the potential for unmeasured confounding variables (e.g., socioeconomic status, political affiliation, or regional economic factors) that may simultaneously influence both ideology and environmental attitudes over time. The language should be softened to emphasize that the data demonstrate a prospective, temporal association rather than a definitive causal link.

issues.description: Inappropriate use of listwise deletion: The use of listwise deletion for a five-year longitudinal study is statistically inappropriate and likely biases the results. Listwise deletion assumes that data are Missing Completely At Random (MCAR), an assumption that is rarely met in multi-year longitudinal survey research due to systematic attrition. Furthermore, it severely reduces statistical power by discarding any participant who missed even a single time point across the five years. The authors should re-analyze the data using modern, robust missing data techniques such as Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML) or Multiple Imputation, which are standard in structural equation modeling, to ensure the parameter estimates are not biased by systematic dropout.

issues.description: Impossible degrees of freedom reported: There appears to be a major error in the reporting of the model fit statistics, specifically the degrees of freedom. The described path model includes three composite variables (SDO, RWA, and environmentalism) measured across five time points, yielding 15 observed variables. The total number of available sample moments (variances and covariances) for 15 variables is 120. It is mathematically impossible for a model with 15 observed variables to have 2,279 degrees of freedom. The authors must clarify whether additional unmentioned variables were included in the model, if item-level data was modeled instead of composite scores, or if this is a typographical error. If item-level data was used, the measurement model details must be fully reported.

issues.quote: We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances. Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings.

issues.subcategory: Contradictory direction of strongest effect between SDO and environmentalism
issues.description: Contradictory direction of strongest effect between SDO and environmentalism: In the Results section, the authors state that "the lagged effect on SDO was stronger than the reverse", which means willingness to sacrifice for the environment has a stronger effect on SDO than SDO has on willingness to sacrifice. However, the very next sentence concludes the exact opposite, stating that "SDO has a stonger influence on environmental attitudes over time than the reverse."

issues.description: Invalid operationalization of behavior: The abstract and results sections claim to evaluate the longitudinal influence of SDO and RWA on people's "willingness to change their behaviour" and "willingness to sacrifice for the environment." However, the actual items detailed in the Methods section only measure general environmental concern and beliefs about whether environmental problems are exaggerated. Because attitudes and concerns do not directly equate to behavioral intentions or willingness to make personal sacrifices, the study fails to operationalize the core behavioral construct it claims to analyze, rendering the major takeaways regarding behavioral change unsupported.

issues.description: Contradictory sample description: The manuscript repeatedly claims its primary novelty and strength is the use of a "large, national probability sample" to test whether previous findings from student samples generalize to the broader population. However, the Methods section explicitly describes a convenience sample of 374 undergraduate students from an introductory psychology pool with an average age of 19. This severe discrepancy completely undermines the study's stated purpose, its claims of generalizability, and the validity of the conclusions drawn about the general population.
